summary: This standards-track document defines the Network Management Datastore Architecture, a framework for datastores that connects YANG data models to protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF. It builds on experience with earlier approaches and separates configuration that is intended from the state a device is actually using. It is the basis for other YANG models written to be NMDA-compatible.

eli5.summary: There is the list of what you asked a device to do, and the list of what it is really doing. This sets up separate places to keep each list.

questions: what is the network management datastore architecture
what is the difference between intended and operational datastores
what does the origin annotation mean in yang
subtitle: A common model of datastores that separates what you configured from what a device is actually using.

tldr.problem: In the original datastore model, configuration and operational state had to be modeled twice in YANG, in separate branches. That duplicated definitions, hurt readability and left the link between the two branches unreadable by machines.
tldr.mechanism: The architecture adds datastores for intended configuration and for operational state, so a data object is defined once and appears in different datastores with different values. Each configuration node in the operational datastore also carries an origin annotation.
tldr.outcome: It gives data models a protocol-agnostic way to talk about configured versus in-use values. It updates RFC 7950.

facts.label: Origin values
facts.value: intended, dynamic, system, learned, default, unknown

today: RFC 8342 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7950, and it has itself been updated by RFC 8808 and RFC 10016. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem With the Original Model
sections.content:
Many network management data objects can have two values: the one configured by a user or application, and the one the device is actually using, called operational state. They can differ because of hardware interaction, protocol interaction, or simply the time it takes to push a change through software and hardware.

The original model required each such object to be modeled twice in YANG, as a config true object and as a config false object. The usual convention was two separate branches at the root of the data tree. The RFC lists the costs: it complicates operations, hurts readability, the relationship between branches is not machine readable, and filter expressions for configuration and for related state differ.

In the new model, a data object is defined once in the YANG schema, and independent instances can appear in different datastores, one for a configured value and one for an operationally used value. It also supports more advanced chains from configuration to operational state, such as inactive configuration and configuration templates.
sections.eli5: Before, you needed one notebook for 'what I asked for' and a totally separate notebook for 'what really happened', and writing down every item twice. Now each item is written once and shows up in both views.

sections.title: The Datastores
sections.content:
A datastore is a conceptual place to store and access information. It might be implemented with files, a database, flash memory or a mix, and it maps to an instantiated YANG data tree. This architecture identifies a set of conceptual datastores but does not require every protocol to expose them all.

The conventional configuration datastores are <running>, <candidate>, <startup> and <intended>. They share one schema, so data can be copied between them.

  • <running> holds the current configuration. It MUST always be a valid configuration data tree and MUST be supported if the device can be configured through conventional datastores.
  • <candidate> can be changed without touching the device's current configuration and later committed to <running>. It may not be supported everywhere.
  • <startup> holds the configuration loaded at boot, and exists only on devices that keep it separate from <running>.
  • <intended> is read-only. It is <running> after configuration transformations such as template expansion and removal of inactive configuration, and is what the system attempts to apply.

Whenever data is written to <running>, the server MUST also immediately update and validate <intended>. For simple implementations the two are identical.
sections.eli5: Think of a draft, a saved copy, the version you are using, and the version after the computer fills in the blanks. Each has its own spot, and the last one is read-only.

sections.title: The Operational State Datastore
sections.content:
<operational> is a read-only datastore with all config true and config false nodes in its schema. It contains system state and all configuration actually used: applied configuration from <intended>, learned configuration, system-provided configuration, default values from the data models, and applied configuration from dynamic configuration datastores. A request always returns the value in use, whatever default the YANG module says, and a missing node means the device is not using it.

Because it reports what is in use, <operational> SHOULD follow the data model's constraints but only semantic constraints MAY be violated, such as when, must, mandatory and unique. Syntactic constraints MUST NOT be violated, and a node that breaks them MUST NOT be returned. It does not persist across reboots.

Three situations are called out. With remnant configuration, nodes for both the old and new configuration may be present until resources are released. With missing resources, such as an interface not currently present, the configuration stays in <intended> but does not appear in <operational>. With system-controlled resources, a resource that appears later picks up matching configuration from <intended>, which then shows up once applied.
sections.eli5: This is the 'what is really happening' list. If you asked for a lamp that is not plugged in, your request stays in your list but not in the 'really on' list.

sections.title: The Origin Annotation
sections.content:
As configuration flows into <operational>, it is conceptually marked with an origin metadata annotation. It applies to all configuration nodes except non-presence containers, and nodes without one inherit it from their parent. Devices SHOULD report the origin that best reflects the source of the configuration in use, and SHOULD use unknown when they cannot tell.

When a value could come from several sources, the YANG description statement SHOULD guide the choice. For example, if the description says a protocol-negotiated value overrides the configured one, the origin is learned even when both values match.
sections.eli5: Each item in the 'really happening' list has a sticker saying where it came from: you, the machine, another machine, or the default.

sections.title: Dynamic Datastores and Defining New Ones
sections.content:
Dynamic configuration datastores hold configuration obtained during operation by interacting with other systems, rather than through the conventional datastores. They are not part of the persistent configuration and are lost on reboot, and they interact with the rest of the system through <operational>. Their schema MAY differ from the conventional one.

Appendix A gives guidelines for defining a new datastore. Each definition should say which YANG modules and nodes apply, how its data is applied and how it interacts with other datastores, which protocols may be used (NETCONF and RESTCONF by default), and which YANG identities represent it. The datastore must have an identity based on ds:datastore, so protocol operations such as <get-data> can reference it. Appendix B sketches an example called ephemeral.
sections.eli5: Some settings come from other machines while the device is running and vanish when it restarts. They get their own place, and there is a checklist for adding more places.

sections.title: What Changes in YANG
sections.content:
This RFC updates RFC 7950 in two places. Section 6.1 refines the accessible tree for some XPath contexts so that, for expressions in nodes representing system state, notifications, and the input and output of RPCs and actions, the tree is all operational state in the server.

Section 6.2 says actions are always invoked in the context of the operational state datastore, and the node an action is invoked on MUST exist there. The RFC does not constrain what an RPC or action does, so one might still modify a datastore.
sections.eli5: When a rule asks 'what is the current situation?', it now looks at the 'really happening' list. Actions are done on things that really exist there.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Appendix C walks through fictional models. In a system example, an interface configured as eth1 has no hardware yet, so it stays in <intended> but not <operational>. A hostname and extra address arrive over DHCP and are shown with origin learned, a default value gets origin default, and a loopback interface lo0 appears with origin system.

In a BGP example, a peer that inherits its local and peer AS numbers from the parent shows those values in <operational>. When the peer is removed, it remains visible there with state closing until its connection is closed and resources are released.
sections.eli5: The examples show a plug that is not in yet, settings borrowed from a neighbor, and a friend who stays on the list until they have really left the room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the architecture has no security impact on the Internet. Its YANG modules only define identities and a metadata annotation, so the YANG security guidelines do not apply.

The one concern is the origin annotation, which may hint that certain control-plane protocols are active on a device. It is accessible only to clients allowed to read the applied configuration values, and administrators should consider its sensitivity when writing access control rules.
sections.eli5: The stickers saying where a setting came from could give away clues about how the device works, so only people allowed to see the settings should see them.

cells: Edits that can be committed to running

items.label: intended
items.desc: Configuration provided by the intended datastore.

items.label: dynamic
items.desc: Configuration from a dynamic configuration datastore.

items.label: system
items.desc: Configuration supplied by the system itself, such as an always-existing loopback interface.

items.label: learned
items.desc: Configuration learned through protocol interactions such as routing protocols and DHCP.

items.label: default
items.desc: A default value from the data model, used only when no other source provides one.

items.label: unknown
items.desc: The system cannot identify the origin.
